27 million for the USSR. 7.4 million for Germany. 1.7 million for Yugoslavia. Every one of those is the ceiling of a published range — and for the Soviet Union the range is 7 million people wide.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The Soviet total is usually given as 20 to 27 million. Russia's own 1993 Academy of Sciences study settles near 26.6 million once deaths from the war's after-effects are counted. The map takes the top of the range.
2/ Germany: 6.9 to 7.4 million. Roughly 4.4–5.3 million military, and 1.5–3 million civilian. The civilian half is where the uncertainty lives — that estimate varies by a factor of two.

3/ Poland's 6 million is the round number everyone repeats. Poland's own Institute of National Remembrance puts it at 5.6 to 5.8 million. Either way it is close to one in six of the pre-war population — the worst share in Europe.

4/ Yugoslavia is the widest gap on the map: 1,027,000 to 1,700,000. The 1.7 million was the official post-war Yugoslav figure. Demographers working on it later got barely over a million. The map shows the political number.

5/ Greece's 807,000 is also a ceiling; the range starts at 507,000. Most of that difference is famine deaths, which are the hardest category in the war to count and the easiest to argue about afterwards.

6/ Hungary 864,000 and Romania 500,000 sit next to each other, and only one is a range — Hungary's runs from 464,000. Border changes are the reason. Which territory you count decides whose dead they were.

7/ Then the exact numbers, exact because they're small. Sweden 2,100. Denmark 6,000. Norway 10,200. Finland 96,800 — more than five times the other three combined, from a country of 3.7 million people.

8/ Read it as a map of estimates, not of deaths. Where the arithmetic is hardest — famine, deportation, the Eastern Front — the uncertainty on a single country exceeds the entire toll of most others.
